name: MRI Investment Payoff
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: From a Physics Curiosity to a Hospital Machine: The MRI Story
lesson.summary: MRI machines that let doctors see inside the body without radiation grew directly out of 1930s and 1940s quantum-mechanical research into how atomic nuclei behave in magnetic fields, a discovery that took roughly half a century to become a piece of hospital equipment.
lesson.body:
Many atomic nuclei, hydrogen being the most relevant one since it is abundant in the water and fat that make up most of the human body, have a quantum mechanical property called spin. A spinning nucleus behaves a bit like a tiny magnet, and when you place it in a strong external magnetic field and hit it with a radio pulse at just the right frequency, it absorbs energy and then releases it again as it settles back down, a phenomenon called nuclear magnetic resonance. The frequency at which this absorption and release happens depends sensitively on the strength of the local magnetic field, which turns out to be the key that makes imaging possible.

This was pure physics when it was first worked out. Isidor Rabi developed methods for measuring the magnetic properties of atomic nuclei in the 1930s, work that earned him the Nobel Prize in 1944. Felix Bloch and Edward Purcell independently extended the technique to observe nuclear magnetic resonance in bulk materials in 1946, and shared the Nobel Prize for it in 1952. None of this research had medicine as its goal. It was an effort to understand the basic quantum mechanical structure of the atomic nucleus, the kind of investigation that, at the time, had no obvious path to a commercial product at all.

The imaging application came decades later. In the 1970s, Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield separately worked out how to add carefully controlled magnetic field gradients across a sample, so that the resonance frequency would vary with position, letting researchers reconstruct a detailed image of the internal structure of an object, including a living human body, from the pattern of nuclear magnetic resonance signals. That insight is what turned a laboratory technique for studying atomic nuclei into magnetic resonance imaging, MRI, and it was significant enough that Lauterbur and Mansfield were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2003, more than fifty years after Rabi's original work on nuclear spin.

That half-century gap is the point. MRI is now a routine part of medicine, used to look at soft tissue, the brain, joints, and tumors, without the ionizing radiation that comes with an X-ray or CT scan, and hospitals around the world run MRI scanners as standard equipment. But the fundamental physics that makes MRI possible was funded and pursued as basic atomic and nuclear physics, with no medical use in sight, and it sat for decades before anyone figured out how to turn it into a picture. Read alongside the GPS chapter, MRI reinforces the same lesson about successful physics bets: the return on curiosity-driven quantum research can be enormous, but it is rarely fast, and it rarely arrives in the form the original researchers imagined. Keep that lesson in mind, because the next several chapters are going to look hard at what happens when that same patient optimism is used to justify bets that do not pay off, or worse, claims that were never true to begin with.
